evidence.claim: A woodland circle near Harpers Crossroads carries a tale of the devil.
evidence.quote: The Devil's Tramping Ground (alternately Devil's Stomping Ground) is a camping spot located in a forest near the Harper's Crossroads area in Bear Creek, North Carolina. It has been the subject of persistent local legends and lore

evidence.claim: Devil’s Tramping Ground Road belongs to North Carolina’s scenic-byway network.
evidence.quote: 42 Devil’s Tramping Ground Road 168

evidence.claim: Its Chatham County setting is gently rolling Piedmont country, with higher hills rising above the general terrain.
evidence.quote: The county lies totally within the Piedmont physiographic region. The topography of the county is generally gently rolling with several higher hills rising above the general terrain.

evidence.claim: NCDOT describes its byways as alternatives to the faster traffic and commercial areas of major highways.
evidence.quote: These byways are intended as an alternative to the faster-paced traffic and commercial areas found along our state’s major highways and interstates.

evidence.claim: Near Harpers Crossroads, a forest clearing called the Devil’s Tramping Ground has inspired persistent local legends.
evidence.quote: The Devil's Tramping Ground (alternately Devil's Stomping Ground) is a camping spot located in a forest near the Harper's Crossroads area in Bear Creek, North Carolina. It has been the subject of persistent local legends and lore

evidence.claim: Journalist John William Harden described the story told by Chatham residents: the devil paces the bare circle while devising trouble for humanity.
evidence.quote: Chatham natives say... that the Devil goes there to walk in circles as he thinks up new means of causing trouble for humanity.

evidence.claim: Journalist John William Harden described the story told by Chatham residents: the devil paces the bare circle while devising trouble for humanity.
evidence.quote: John William Harden (1903–1985) of Greensboro, N.C., journalist, newspaper editor, author

evidence.claim: Pittsboro’s courthouse occupies a traffic circle at the center of town.
evidence.quote: It sits at the center of town in the middle of a traffic circle.

evidence.claim: Farther along the journey, Harpers Crossroads marks the meeting of NC 902 and Siler City Glendon Road.
evidence.quote: It is located at the intersection of State Highway 902, and Siler City Glendon Rd.

evidence.claim: The woodland circle lies near this crossroads in the Bear Creek area.
evidence.quote: located in a forest near the Harper's Crossroads area in Bear Creek, North Carolina.

evidence.claim: Pittsboro’s town plan began with a land problem.
evidence.quote: The Chatham County Court House was built on land belonging to Mial Scurlock, but in 1787 the legislature declared that a town could not be established on Scurlock's land.

evidence.claim: In 1787, the legislature ruled out establishing a town on Mial Scurlock’s property, where the courthouse had been built.
evidence.quote: The Chatham County Court House was built on land belonging to Mial Scurlock, but in 1787 the legislature declared that a town could not be established on Scurlock's land.

evidence.claim: The trustees bought adjoining land from William Petty and laid out the town there; Pittsboro officially became the county seat that year.
evidence.quote: The town's trustees instead purchased adjacent land belonging to William Petty and laid out the town. That same year, Pittsboro was officially named the county seat.

evidence.claim: Its name honors William Pitt the Younger, while Chatham County honors his father.
evidence.quote: Although Chatham County is named for William Pitt, 1st Earl of Chatham, Pittsboro is named for his son, William Pitt the Younger.

evidence.claim: The town was considered for both the state university and the state capital.
evidence.quote: Pittsboro was once considered as a site for both the University of North Carolina and the state capital.

evidence.claim: As county seat, it became a center for trade and local government, drawing farmers into town on weekends to do business.
evidence.quote: As the county seat, Pittsboro has been a center of trade and local government, including the courts. Many farmers would come into town on the weekend for trade.

evidence.claim: A three-stage cupola rises above the Chatham County Courthouse’s two-story classical portico.
evidence.quote: It features a two-story classical portico crowned with a distinctive three-stage cupola.

evidence.claim: Built in 1881, the rectangular brick courthouse stands in the traffic circle at Pittsboro’s center.
evidence.quote: It sits at the center of town in the middle of a traffic circle. It was built in 1881 for $10,666 and is a two-story rectangular brick structure

evidence.claim: The Works Progress Administration added a one-story extension in the 1930s, and extensive renovations followed in 1959. The courthouse entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1979.
evidence.quote:
A one-story addition was built in the 1930s by the Works Progress Administration. In 1959, extensive renovations were performed on the building.
It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1979.

evidence.claim: A fire during renovation badly damaged the building in March 2010.
evidence.quote: A fire on March 24, 2010, did great damage to the building which was in the midst of another renovation.

evidence.claim: The restored courthouse reopened in April 2013, with a county-history exhibit downstairs and a courtroom upstairs.
evidence.quote: The restored building reopened April 20, 2013 with an exhibit covering Chatham County history on the first floor and a courtroom on the second.

evidence.claim: The portico rises two stories beneath a three-stage cupola.
evidence.quote: It features a two-story classical portico crowned with a distinctive three-stage cupola.

evidence.claim: The Devil’s Tramping Ground is a woodland circle near Harpers Crossroads whose reputation rests on local lore.
evidence.quote: The Devil's Tramping Ground (alternately Devil's Stomping Ground) is a camping spot located in a forest near the Harper's Crossroads area in Bear Creek, North Carolina. It has been the subject of persistent local legends and lore

evidence.claim: Journalist and author John William Harden recorded Chatham residents’ story of the devil walking in circles here while thinking up ways to cause trouble for humanity.
evidence.quote: Chatham natives say... that the Devil goes there to walk in circles as he thinks up new means of causing trouble for humanity.

evidence.claim: Journalist and author John William Harden recorded Chatham residents’ story of the devil walking in circles here while thinking up ways to cause trouble for humanity.
evidence.quote: John William Harden (1903–1985) of Greensboro, N.C., journalist, newspaper editor, author

evidence.claim: In Harden’s telling, that pacing takes place on the bare circle during the night.
evidence.quote: There, sometimes during the dark of night, the Majesty of the Underworld of Evil silently tramps around that bare circle

evidence.claim: The place also appears in Poppy Z. Brite’s horror novels Lost Souls and Drawing Blood.
evidence.quote: The Devil's Tramping Ground is mentioned in two horror novels by Poppy Z. Brite: Lost Souls and Drawing Blood.

evidence.claim: Both novels are set at least partly in Missing Mile, a fictional North Carolina city. The real place is also called Devil’s Stomping Ground.
evidence.quote: Both these novels take place, at least in part, in the fictional North Carolina city of Missing Mile

evidence.claim: The real place is also called Devil’s Stomping Ground.
evidence.quote: The Devil's Tramping Ground (alternately Devil's Stomping Ground)
